claim: The actin cortex consists of a thin actin meshwork bound to the inner cytosolic face of the plasma membrane by various anchor proteins.
source: The actin cortex consists of a thin actin meshwork bound to the inner cytosolic face of the plasma membrane by various anchor proteins (Morone et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Morone et al., 2006

claim: The actin cortex plays a pivotal role in providing mechanical stability to the cell membrane.
source: It plays a pivotal role in providing mechanical stability to the cell membrane, and in controlling cell shape changes during cell locomotion and cell division (Wessells et al., 1971; Bray and White, 1988; Diz-Muñoz et al., 2010; Sedzinski et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Wessells et al., 1971; Bray and White, 1988; Diz-Muñoz et al., 2010; Sedzinski et al., 2011

claim: The actin cortex controls cell shape changes during cell locomotion and cell division.
source: It plays a pivotal role in providing mechanical stability to the cell membrane, and in controlling cell shape changes during cell locomotion and cell division (Wessells et al., 1971; Bray and White, 1988; Diz-Muñoz et al., 2010; Sedzinski et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Wessells et al., 1971; Bray and White, 1988; Diz-Muñoz et al., 2010; Sedzinski et al., 2011

claim: Many features of the actin cortex rely on proper functioning of the actin motor myosin II.
source: Many of these features rely on proper functioning of the actin motor myosin II (De Lozanne and Spudich, 1987; Cramer and Mitchison, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to De Lozanne and Spudich, 1987; Cramer and Mitchison, 1995

claim: Myosin II in the actin cortex functions as assemblies of motor proteins forming anti-parallely arranged bipolar filaments (myofilaments) with motor domains on both filament ends.
source: Myosin II in the actin cortex functions as assemblies of motor proteins forming anti-parallely arranged bipolar filaments (myofilaments) with motor domains on both filament ends ((Verkhovsky and Borisy, 1993; Verkhovsky et al., 1995), Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Verkhovsky and Borisy, 1993; Verkhovsky et al., 1995 and schematic in Figure 1A

claim: Myofilaments are the force generator necessary for cell cortex remodeling and actomyosin ring constriction during cytokinesis.
source: Besides being the force generator necessary for cell cortex remodeling and actomyosin ring constriction during cytokinesis, there is evidence that myofilaments also contribute to actin filament turnover during cyotkinesis (Burgess, 2005; Guha et al., 2005; Murthy and Wadsworth, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Burgess, 2005; Guha et al., 2005; Murthy and Wadsworth, 2005

claim: There is evidence that myofilaments contribute to actin filament turnover during cytokinesis.
source: Besides being the force generator necessary for cell cortex remodeling and actomyosin ring constriction during cytokinesis, there is evidence that myofilaments also contribute to actin filament turnover during cyotkinesis (Burgess, 2005; Guha et al., 2005; Murthy and Wadsworth, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Burgess, 2005; Guha et al., 2005; Murthy and Wadsworth, 2005

claim: The microscopic mechanism of the interaction between individual myofilaments and membrane-bound actin filaments is not understood.
source: In all these processes, the microscopic mechanism of the interaction between individual myofilaments and membrane-bound actin filaments is not understood.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the field

claim: Previous in vitro studies focused on myosin-induced actin structure formation on a mesoscopic scale, rather than on the interaction between actin and individual myofilaments.
source: However, these studies focused on myosin-induced actin structure formation on a mesoscopic scale, rather than on the interaction between actin and individual myofilaments.
evidence: Characterization of prior work in the field, supported by citations to Backouche et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2007; Schaller et al., 2010; Kohler et al., 2011; Soares e Silva et al., 2011; Gordon et al., 2012; Reymann et al., 2012

claim: Membrane-bound minimal actin systems have only recently begun to be functionally reconstituted.
source: In addition, membrane-bound minimal actin systems have only recently begun to be functionally reconstituted (Vogel and Schwille, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vogel and Schwille, 2012

claim: The minimal actin cortex (MAC) consists of actin filaments coupled to a supported lipid bilayer via biotin neutravidin bonds.
source: To mimic the cell cortex, we developed a 'minimal actin cortex' (MAC) consisting of actin filaments coupled to a supported lipid bilayer via biotin neutravidin bonds (Figure 1A).
evidence: Experimental design described in text and shown in Figure 1A schematic

claim: By varying the amount of biotinylated lipids present in the lipid bilayer, control over the density of the actin layer can be achieved.
source: By varying the amount of biotinylated lipids present in the lipid bilayer, we have control over the density of the actin layer (Figure 1B).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 1B with different actin densities

claim: Synthetic myofilaments have a typical length of 500–600 nm.
source: Rabbit muscle myosin II was purified and reassembled forming bipolar synthetic myofilaments with a typical length of 500–600 nm (Figure 1C).
evidence: Experimental measurement shown in Figure 1C length distribution with median of 0.56 µm

claim: MACs with various actin densities showed dynamic rearrangement of actin filaments after addition of myofilaments in an ATP-dependent manner.
source: Time lapse imaging of MACs with various actin densities using total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy (TIRFM) showed a dynamic rearrangement of the actin filaments, and subsequently the formation of actomyosin foci in an ATP-dependent manner immediately after addition of myofilaments (Figure 1D, Movie 1).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 1D and Movie 1

claim: Actin pattern formation occurred at ATP concentrations between 0.1–1 µM in systems where ATP is enzymatically regenerated.
source: Actin pattern formation occurred at ATP concentrations between 0.1–1 µM in systems where ATP is enzymatically regenerated (Table 1) in 94% of the experiments (n = 45 experiments).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Table 1 with n=45 experiments

claim: At higher and lower ATP concentrations than 0.1-1 µM, actin pattern formation in the MAC is absent.
source: At higher and lower ATP concentrations, actin pattern formation in the MAC is absent.
evidence: Experimental observation supported by Table 1 data

claim: Actin structure formation after ATP depletion has been reported for experiments using actin and myofilaments in solution.
source: Actin structure formation after ATP depletion has been also reported for experiments using actin and myofilaments in solution (Smith et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith et al., 2007

claim: At low ATP concentrations, myofilaments were predicted to function as active temporary crosslinkers, which may drive self-assembly of actin filaments into actin clusters.
source: At low ATP concentrations, myofilaments were predicted to function as active temporary crosslinkers, which may drive self-assembly of actin filaments into actin clusters.
evidence: Inference based on experimental observations and prior work

claim: Myofilament addition to low density MACs displayed breakage events and compaction of actin filaments, resulting in their shortening over time in all experiments.
source: Strikingly, myofilament addition to low density MACs displayed breakage events and compaction of actin filaments, resulting in their shortening over time in all experiments (n = 21, Figure 2A–C, Movie 2).
evidence: Experimental observation with n=21 experiments shown in Figure 2A-C and Movie 2

claim: After 20 min, the majority of the actin filaments have been shortened to, on average, half of their original length.
source: After 20 min, the majority of the actin filaments have been shortened to, on average, half of their original length, and most of the fragments coalesced into single foci (Figure 2A,B, Movie 2).
evidence: Experimental measurement shown in Figure 2B length distributions at different time points

claim: Actin filaments remained intact when imaged in the absence of myofilaments.
source: Note that actin filaments remained intact when imaged in the absence of myofilaments (data not shown).
evidence: Control experiment mentioned in text

claim: Upon myofilament addition, actin filaments frequently showed deformations prior to actin filament breakage.
source: Upon myofilament addition, actin filaments frequently showed deformations prior to actin filament breakage (Figure 2C, yellow arrowheads, Movie 3), indicating that force is exerted by the myofilaments and stress along the actin filament may build up until the actin filament breaks.
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 2C and Movie 3

claim: Force is exerted by the myofilaments and stress along the actin filament may build up until the actin filament breaks.
source: Upon myofilament addition, actin filaments frequently showed deformations prior to actin filament breakage (Figure 2C, yellow arrowheads, Movie 3), indicating that force is exerted by the myofilaments and stress along the actin filament may build up until the actin filament breaks.
evidence: Inference from observed deformations prior to breakage

claim: Exposure of actin/fascin bundles to myofilaments can induce their disassembling and severing.
source: Similarly, recent evidence implied that exposure of actin/fascin bundles to myofilaments can induce their disassembling and severing by an unknown process (Backouche et al., 2006; Haviv et al., 2008; Thoresen et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Backouche et al., 2006; Haviv et al., 2008; Thoresen et al., 2011

claim: An increase in fluorescence intensity along the remaining actin filament is often observed after a fragmentation event.
source: Furthermore, an increase in fluorescence intensity along the remaining actin filament is often observed after a fragmentation event (Figure 2C, white arrowheads, Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 2C, D, and E

claim: The fluorescence intensity proximal to the breakage site is approximately twice as high compared to the rest of the actin filament.
source: The fluorescence intensity proximal to the breakage site is approximately twice as high compared to the rest of the actin filament, suggesting that the fragment is dragged along the remaining actin filament by the myofilaments leading to its compaction (Figure 2C–E, Movie 3).
evidence: Experimental measurement shown in Figure 2D and E intensity profile

claim: The fragment is dragged along the remaining actin filament by the myofilaments leading to its compaction.
source: The fluorescence intensity proximal to the breakage site is approximately twice as high compared to the rest of the actin filament, suggesting that the fragment is dragged along the remaining actin filament by the myofilaments leading to its compaction (Figure 2C–E, Movie 3).
evidence: Inference from the observed increase in fluorescence intensity

claim: Fragmentation and compaction contribute to the observed coalescence of actin fragments into single foci during the dynamic rearrangement of the actin filaments.
source: We propose that fragmentation and compaction contribute to the observed coalescence of actin fragments into single foci during the dynamic rearrangement of the actin filaments (Figures 1D and 2A, Movies 1 and 2).
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on experimental observations in Figures 1D and 2A

claim: 68% of the individually observed myofilaments displayed directed movement.
source: 68% of the individually observed myofilaments displayed directed movement and 50% exhibited fragmentation and compaction of an actin filament (total number of myofilaments = 152; 7 experiments).
evidence: Experimental data from 152 myofilaments across 7 experiments

claim: 50% of individually observed myofilaments exhibited fragmentation and compaction of an actin filament.
source: 68% of the individually observed myofilaments displayed directed movement and 50% exhibited fragmentation and compaction of an actin filament (total number of myofilaments = 152; 7 experiments).
evidence: Experimental data from 152 myofilaments across 7 experiments

claim: 95% of the observed myofilaments that showed both fragmentation and compaction displayed directed movement along the actin filaments.
source: In cases where both fragmentation and compaction occurred, 95% of the observed myofilaments showed directed movement along the actin filaments, while 5% remained stationary at their original binding site (total number of fragmenting myofilaments = 75; seven experiments).
evidence: Experimental data from 75 fragmenting myofilaments across 7 experiments

claim: 5% of myofilaments that showed fragmentation and compaction remained stationary at their original binding site.
source: In cases where both fragmentation and compaction occurred, 95% of the observed myofilaments showed directed movement along the actin filaments, while 5% remained stationary at their original binding site (total number of fragmenting myofilaments = 75; seven experiments).
evidence: Experimental data from 75 fragmenting myofilaments across 7 experiments

claim: At high ATP concentrations, processive movement of myofilaments was barely visible, and fragmentation of actin filaments was absent.
source: In contrast, at high ATP concentrations, processive movement of myofilaments was barely visible, and fragmentation of actin filaments was absent (supplementary text in 'Material and methods', Figure 5, Movie 5).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 5 and Movie 5

claim: Shortly after binding of myofilaments, actin filaments deformed and eventually broke.
source: Shortly after binding of myofilaments, actin filaments deformed and eventually broke, indicating that the force generated by a single myofilament is sufficient to break an actin filament (Figure 3A, yellow arrowheads, Movie 4).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 3A and Movie 4

claim: The force generated by a single myofilament is sufficient to break an actin filament.
source: Shortly after binding of myofilaments, actin filaments deformed and eventually broke, indicating that the force generated by a single myofilament is sufficient to break an actin filament (Figure 3A, yellow arrowheads, Movie 4).
evidence: Inference from single molecule observations of breakage

claim: Actin fragments are dragged along the remaining actin filaments by the myofilaments during their movement.
source: The detected increase in the fluorescence intensity of actin filaments implies that actin fragments are further dragged along the remaining actin filaments by the myofilaments during their movement (Figure 3A,D, Movie 4).
evidence: Inference from fluorescence intensity increase shown in Figure 3A and Movie 4

claim: The velocity of myofilaments fluctuates during their movement along the actin filament.
source: The velocity fluctuates during the movement of the myofilament along the actin filament (Figure 3C, red curve), whereby acceleration events (Figure 3C, red arrowheads) are closely followed by an increase in the actin fluorescence, indicating that a breakage event occurred (Figure 3C, black arrows, blue and black curve).
evidence: Experimental measurement shown in Figure 3C velocity curve

claim: Acceleration events of myofilaments are closely followed by an increase in the actin fluorescence, indicating that a breakage event occurred.
source: The velocity fluctuates during the movement of the myofilament along the actin filament (Figure 3C, red curve), whereby acceleration events (Figure 3C, red arrowheads) are closely followed by an increase in the actin fluorescence, indicating that a breakage event occurred (Figure 3C, black arrows, blue and black curve).
evidence: Experimental observation correlating velocity and fluorescence changes in Figure 3C

claim: Phases of increasing tension between the ends of the myofilament lead to deformation of the actin filament and coincide with a decrease in velocity.
source: We hypothesize that phases of increasing tension between the ends of the myofilament lead to deformation of the actin filament and coincide with a decrease in velocity, while the phases of tension release immediately after actin filament breakage may result in acceleration of the myofilament (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Hypothesis based on observed velocity fluctuations and breakage events

claim: Phases of tension release immediately after actin filament breakage may result in acceleration of the myofilament.
source: We hypothesize that phases of increasing tension between the ends of the myofilament lead to deformation of the actin filament and coincide with a decrease in velocity, while the phases of tension release immediately after actin filament breakage may result in acceleration of the myofilament (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Hypothesis based on observed velocity fluctuations and breakage events

claim: The myosin filament aligns parallel to the actin filament and interacts with it via the myosin heads.
source: In order to explain the buckling and eventual breakage of the actin filament, we propose the following model: The myosin filament aligns parallel to the actin filament and interacts with it via the myosin heads ((Sellers and Kachar, 1990), Figure 3D).
evidence: Proposed model based on citation to Sellers and Kachar, 1990 and shown in Figure 3D

claim: One end of the myofilament (the 'leading end') is oriented towards the actin plus end and can walk along the actin filament while hydrolyzing ATP.
source: One end of the myofilament, which we will refer to as the 'leading end', is oriented towards the actin plus end (barbed end), as the filaments in a muscle, and can therefore walk along the actin filament while hydrolyzing ATP (Figure 3D).
evidence: Proposed model mechanism shown in Figure 3D

claim: The trailing end of the myofilament is separated from the leading end by the approximately 160 nm long bare zone without myosin heads.
source: The other end of the myofilament, which we will refer to as the 'trailing end', separated from the leading end by the approximately 160 nm long bare zone (Al-Khayat et al., 2010) without myosin heads, is oriented in the opposite direction.
evidence: Structural information supported by citation to Al-Khayat et al., 2010

claim: The trailing end's opposite orientation results in a much slower directed motion towards the actin plus end.
source: While the trailing end still interacts with the actin filament, its opposite orientation results in a much slower directed motion towards the actin plus end (Spudich et al., 1985; Sellers and Kachar, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to Spudich et al., 1985; Sellers and Kachar, 1990

claim: Every myosin head independently follows the biochemical cycle consisting of ATP hydrolysis, binding to actin, powerstroke accompanied by phosphate dissociation, ADP dissociation, ATP binding, and finally detachment from actin.
source: Every myosin head independently follows the biochemical cycle consisting of ATP hydrolysis, binding to actin, powerstroke accompanied by phosphate dissociation, ADP dissociation, ATP binding, and finally detachment from actin ((Howard, 2001), Figure 8).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation to Howard, 2001 and shown in Figure 8

claim: The myofilament trailing end functions mainly as a source of friction (an effective 'brake').
source: The myofilament trailing end functions mainly as a source of friction (an effective 'brake'), but is also moved towards the plus end by the pulling force exerted by the leading end (Figure 3D).
evidence: Proposed mechanism shown in Figure 3D model

claim: Tension builds up within the myofilament and is transferred onto the actin filament as a compressive force.
source: Since mainly the leading end is actively moving and the trailing end is either passively pulled (pst=0) or contributes only weakly to its own motion (pst=0.1), tension builds up within the myofilament, and is transferred onto the actin filament as a compressive force.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on model assumptions

claim: If sufficiently high, the compressive force can cause buckling, and finally breakage, of the actin filament.
source: If sufficiently high, this compressive force can cause buckling, and finally breakage, of the actin filament (Figure 3D).
evidence: Proposed mechanism shown in Figure 3D model

claim: After the breakage, the leading end can move unhindered further towards the plus end, while dragging along the broken-off part of the actin filament attached to the trailing end.
source: After the breakage, the leading end can move unhindered further towards the plus end, while dragging along the broken-off part of the actin filament attached to the trailing end (Figure 3D).
evidence: Proposed mechanism shown in Figure 3D model

claim: The force needed to buckle and break an actin filament is approximately 23 pN.
source: In order to estimate the force needed to break an actin filament, we model the filaments as flexible rods with bending rigidity EI = 60 nN μm2, determined from the persistence length of actin: lp = EI/(kT) = 15 μm (Yanagida et al., 1984). The force needed to buckle and break a filament is F = π2 EI/l2. With the length l of the myofilament bare zone of 160 nm, this gives a force of 23 pN.
evidence: Calculated from physical model using known actin persistence length from Yanagida et al., 1984

claim: The persistence length of actin is 15 μm.
source: In order to estimate the force needed to break an actin filament, we model the filaments as flexible rods with bending rigidity EI = 60 nN μm2, determined from the persistence length of actin: lp = EI/(kT) = 15 μm (Yanagida et al., 1984).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yanagida et al., 1984

claim: Simulations show that the tension force increases with decreasing ATP concentration, reaching forces necessary for breakage only at low (lesser than ∼3 µM) ATP concentrations.
source: We note that the tension force increases with decreasing ATP concentration, reaching forces necessary for breakage only at low (lesser than ∼3 µM) ATP concentrations, in agreement with the experiments (Figure 4A, see also Table 1).
evidence: Simulation results shown in Figure 4A compared with experimental data in Table 1

claim: At low ATP concentrations, the filament curvature steadily increased, reaching the critical curvature of breaking of 5.6 µm−1.
source: When the actin filament was allowed to bend in simulations at the point where the buckling force of 23 pN was reached (Figure 4B), thus releasing the excess tension, the filament curvature steadily increased at low ATP concentrations, reaching the critical curvature of breaking of 5.6 µm−1 ((Arai et al., 1999), Figure 7A).
evidence: Simulation results shown in Figure 4B and 7A, critical curvature from Arai et al., 1999

claim: The critical curvature of actin breaking is 5.6 µm−1.
source: When the actin filament was allowed to bend in simulations at the point where the buckling force of 23 pN was reached (Figure 4B), thus releasing the excess tension, the filament curvature steadily increased at low ATP concentrations, reaching the critical curvature of breaking of 5.6 µm−1 ((Arai et al., 1999), Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arai et al., 1999

claim: At intermediate ATP concentrations, the actin curvature fluctuated, at times exceeding the curvature threshold.
source: At intermediate ATP concentrations, the actin curvature fluctuated, at times exceeding the curvature threshold (Figures 4C and 7B).
evidence: Simulation results shown in Figures 4C and 7B

claim: At higher ATP concentrations, the threshold force was reached for too short periods for the filament to be bent to the breakage point.
source: At higher ATP concentrations, the threshold force was reached for too short periods for the filament to be bent to the breakage point (Figures 4D and 7C).
evidence: Simulation results shown in Figures 4D and 7C

claim: The simulation results do not depend significantly on whether the myosin heads on the trailing end perform steps (pst=0.1) or not (pst=0).
source: The results do not depend significantly on whether the myosin heads on the trailing end perform steps (pst=0.1) or not (pst=0).
evidence: Comparison of simulation results with different parameter values

claim: The simulations support the idea that in the ATP concentration range used in the experiments, the differences in the interactions of the trailing and leading ends of the myofilament with actin can generate compressive forces on the actin filament.
source: The simulations thus support the idea that in the ATP concentration range used in the experiments, the differences in the interactions of the trailing and leading ends of the myofilament with actin can generate compressive forces on the actin filament, and that these forces are sufficiently high to bend and break the actin filament.
evidence: Conclusion from simulation results

claim: The forces generated by differences in the interactions of the trailing and leading ends are sufficiently high to bend and break the actin filament.
source: The simulations thus support the idea that in the ATP concentration range used in the experiments, the differences in the interactions of the trailing and leading ends of the myofilament with actin can generate compressive forces on the actin filament, and that these forces are sufficiently high to bend and break the actin filament.
evidence: Conclusion from simulation results

claim: To bend and break the actin filament, the myofilament has to be attached to the actin for sufficient time.
source: To bend and break the actin filament, the myofilament has to be attached to the actin for sufficient time, and sufficient force has to be generated, requiring a certain mean number of heads being attached to actin at any given time.
evidence: Inference from model requirements

claim: Sufficient force has to be generated to bend and break the actin filament, requiring a certain mean number of heads being attached to actin at any given time.
source: To bend and break the actin filament, the myofilament has to be attached to the actin for sufficient time, and sufficient force has to be generated, requiring a certain mean number of heads being attached to actin at any given time.
evidence: Inference from model requirements

claim: A large fraction of myosin heads must be in the bound state to generate sufficient force.
source: Given the small number of interacting myosin heads this translates to a requirement that a large fraction of heads is in the bound state.
evidence: Inference from model requirements

claim: In the experimental assay, a large fraction of bound myosin heads was achieved with low ATP concentrations.
source: In our assay this was achieved with low ATP concentrations.
evidence: Experimental design choice based on model requirements

claim: It is tempting to speculate that actin breakage by myofilaments in vivo is governed by the ATP level in the cell.
source: It is tempting to speculate that actin breakage by myofilaments in vivo is governed by the ATP level in the cell.
evidence: Speculation about in vivo relevance

claim: Recent evidence exists that ATP levels vary significantly inside living cells.
source: Recent evidence exists that ATP levels indeed vary significantly inside living cells (Imamura et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Imamura et al., 2009

claim: Physiological ATP concentrations are usually found in the millimolar range.
source: However, physiological ATP concentrations, derived from methods that provide averaged ATP levels with no high spatial and temporal resolution from cell extracts, are usually found in the millimolar range (Beis and Newsholme, 1975).
evidence: Supported by citation to Beis and Newsholme, 1975

claim: Skeletal muscle myosin II has a lower duty ratio and is therefore less processive than non-muscle myosin in cells.
source: Here it is important to mention that skeletal muscle myosin II (used in this study) has a lower duty ratio and is therefore less processive than non-muscle myosin in cells (Harris and Warshaw, 1993; Wang et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Harris and Warshaw, 1993; Wang et al., 2003

claim: By lowering the ATP concentration in the assay, the duty ratio of myofilaments was increased and thereby made them more processive, similar to non-muscle myosin.
source: By lowering the ATP concentration in our assay, we increased the duty ratio of our myofilaments and thereby made them more processive (supplementary text in 'Material and methods', Figure 5, Movie 5), similar to non-muscle myosin, which is in line with previous studies (Humphrey et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2007; Soares e Silva et al., 2011).
evidence: Experimental approach supported by Figure 5, Movie 5, and citations to Humphrey et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2007; Soares e Silva et al., 2011

claim: Processivity of myofilaments in animal cells may be controlled by phosphorylation of myosin light chains through other proteins that modify the kinetic rates of the biochemical cycle.
source: Moreover, processivity of myofilaments in animal cells may be also controlled by phosphorylation of myosin light chains through other proteins that modify the kinetic rates of the biochemical cycle and thereby increase the duty ratio of the myosins shifting the observed behavior to a region of high physiological ATP concentrations (Tan et al., 1992; DeBiasio et al., 1996; Matsumura et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tan et al., 1992; DeBiasio et al., 1996; Matsumura et al., 2001

claim: The simulations show that the model of interaction between the actin and myosin filaments is plausible given the quantitative parameter values known from literature.
source: Our simulations show that the model of interaction between the actin and myosin filaments described in the text is plausible given the quantitative parameter values known from literature (rate constants).
evidence: Conclusion from simulation results using literature-derived parameters

claim: Sufficient force needed to bend and break the actin filament can be generated by a single myofilament, assuming only the difference in the interaction between the leading and trailing myofilament ends.
source: Most importantly, it shows that sufficient force needed to bend and break the actin filament can be generated by a single myofilament, assuming only the difference in the interaction between the leading and trailing myofilament ends (making a step vs not making a step).
evidence: Conclusion from simulation results

claim: Neither actin nor myosin attachment to a support or any other rigid structure is necessary for the observed process.
source: This result implies that neither actin nor myosin attachment to a support or any other rigid structure is necessary for the observed process.
evidence: Inference from simulation results

claim: The forces act within a single myofilament.
source: The forces act within a single myofilament.
evidence: Conclusion from model mechanism

claim: Binding of the actin filaments to the membrane provides confinement of the filaments to a plane, without rigidly tethering the filaments to a support or a scaffold.
source: Binding of the actin filaments to the membrane provides confinement of the filaments to a plane, without rigidly tethering the filaments to a support or a scaffold.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental design

claim: The motion of actin is only restricted by the effectively higher viscosity of the membrane compared to the buffer solution.
source: The motion of actin is only restricted by the effectively higher viscosity of the membrane compared to the buffer solution.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental system properties

claim: The findings show that myofilaments fragment and compact membrane-bound actin in the minimal system.
source: In conclusion, our findings show the distinct functions that myosin motors can execute. In our minimal system, myofilaments fragment and compact membrane-bound actin.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Single myofilaments can interact with actin in such a way that sufficient force can be generated to break the filament, without either the myofilament or the actin being firmly attached to a solid support or scaffold.
source: We directly show that single myofilaments can interact with actin in such a way that sufficient force can be generated to break the filament, without either the myofilament or the actin being firmly attached to a solid support or scaffold.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Fragmentation and compaction by myofilaments contributes to the observed large-scale pattern formation of actomyosin networks in other in vitro systems.
source: We suggest that fragmentation and compaction by myofilaments contributes to the observed large-scale pattern formation of actomyosin networks also in other in vitro systems (Backouche et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2007; Soares e Silva et al., 2011; Gordon et al., 2012).
evidence: Proposed generalization supported by citations to Backouche et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2007; Soares e Silva et al., 2011; Gordon et al., 2012

claim: In vivo breakage of actin bundles has been shown to occur in neuronal growth cones in a myosin II dependent manner.
source: In vivo breakage of actin bundles has been shown to occur in neuronal growth cones in a myosin II dependent manner, and is thought to be important for recycling actin (Medeiros et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Medeiros et al., 2006

claim: The observed fragmentation and compaction of membrane-bound actin filaments by myosins may serve as a possible general mechanism for actin turnover and actin cell cortex remodeling.
source: We propose that the observed fragmentation and compaction of membrane-bound actin filaments by myosins in our in vitro system may serve as a possible general mechanism for actin turnover and actin cell cortex remodeling.
evidence: Proposed general mechanism based on experimental findings

claim: Single muscle myosin II motors are traditionally described as non-processive motors.
source: Traditionally, single muscle myosin II motors are described as non-processive motors (Howard, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Howard, 2001

claim: By assembling myosin motors into filaments, the myofilaments become processive due to the coupling of a higher number of myosin heads that are in contact with the actin filament.
source: By assembling myosin motors into filaments, the myofilaments become processive due to the coupling of a higher number of myosin heads that are in contact with the actin filament.
evidence: Established knowledge about myofilament behavior

claim: In the minimal system, directed movement accompanied by actin filament fragmentation only occurred at low ATP concentrations between 0.1–1 µM.
source: In our minimal system directed movement accompanied by actin filament fragmentation only occurred at low ATP concentrations between 0.1–1 µM (Figure 3, Table 1, Movie 3).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 3, Table 1, and Movie 3

claim: Lower ATP concentrations are expected to increase the duration of the actin-bound post-working stroke state of the myosin head, thus increasing the duty ratio and processivity.
source: The lower ATP concentrations are expected to increase the duration of the actin-bound post-working stroke state of the myosin head, thus increasing the duty ratio and processivity (Howard, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Howard, 2001

claim: Extremely low ATP concentrations are not sufficient for myosin motor activity.
source: Extremely low ATP concentrations are on the other hand not sufficient for myosin motor activity.
evidence: Established knowledge about myosin motor requirements

claim: Low ATP trajectories of myofilaments are on average longer than high ATP trajectories indicating a higher processivity at low ATP conditions.
source: Comparison of the trajectories illustrates that low ATP trajectories are on average longer than high ATP trajectories indicating a higher processivity at low ATP conditions (Figure 5, Movie 5).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 5 and Movie 5

claim: The number of tracked myofilaments at low ATP concentration with a dwell time greater than 900 ms was more than six times higher than at high ATP concentration.
source: Moreover the number of tracked myofilaments at low ATP concentration with a dwell time greater than 900 ms was more than six times higher than at high ATP concentration suggesting a higher duty ratio at low ATP levels (n = 681 at low ATP, n = 102 at high ATP; Figure 5, Movie 5).
evidence: Experimental data with n=681 at low ATP and n=102 at high ATP shown in Figure 5 and Movie 5

claim: High ATP concentrations lead to a faster detachment of myofilaments from actin filaments than at low ATP concentrations.
source: High ATP concentrations therefore lead to a faster detachment of myofilaments from actin filaments than at low ATP concentrations (Movie 5).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Movie 5

claim: The increase in processivity due to ATP deprivation is necessary for the processive movement and a prerequisite for fragmentation and compaction of actin filaments.
source: We propose that the increase in processivity due to ATP deprivation is necessary for the processive movement and a prerequisite for fragmentation and compaction of actin filaments.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on experimental observations

claim: The myosin step size is 5 nm.
source: The myosin step size is d = 5 nm (Howard, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Howard, 2001

claim: The myosin head stiffness is 1 pN nm−1.
source: We performed simulations of this model, describing the attached myosin head as a spring with a spring constant equal to the myosin head stiffness κ = 1 pN nm−1 (Kaya and Higuchi, 2010), and equilibrate all forces after every step and every detachment of a myosin head.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kaya and Higuchi, 2010

claim: There are approximately 30 interacting myosin heads per filament.
source: From the AFM image of the myofilament (Figure 1C) and the known myofilament structure (Woodhead et al., 2005), we estimated that there are nm = 30 interacting myosin heads per filament.
evidence: Estimated from AFM image in Figure 1C and citation to Woodhead et al., 2005

claim: The median length of the myofilaments determined with AFM was 560 nm.
source: The median length of the myofilaments determined with AFM was 560 nm (Figure 1C).
evidence: Experimental measurement shown in Figure 1C

claim: The length of the bare zone without myosin heads in the central part of the myofilament is 160 nm.
source: Assuming the length of the bare zone without myosin heads in the central part of the myofilament to be 160 nm (Al-Khayat et al., 2010), both ends of the myofilament are 200 nm long.
evidence: Supported by citation to Al-Khayat et al., 2010

claim: There are four myosin head pairs around the myofilament circumference per every 14.5 nm.
source: With four myosin head pairs around the myofilament circumference per every 14.5 nm (Woodhead et al., 2005), there are on average 110 head pairs on each myofilament.
evidence: Supported by citation to Woodhead et al., 2005

claim: There are on average 110 head pairs on each myofilament.
source: With four myosin head pairs around the myofilament circumference per every 14.5 nm (Woodhead et al., 2005), there are on average 110 head pairs on each myofilament.
evidence: Calculated from structural information from Woodhead et al., 2005

claim: Only those myosin heads oriented towards one side (one quarter) can interact with the actin filament.
source: Assuming further that only those heads oriented towards one side, that is, one quarter, can interact with the actin filament, and that only one head of the head pair is favorably oriented to interact, we estimate the average number of interacting heads as 30 per myofilament.
evidence: Assumption used in model calculation

claim: Only one head of the head pair is favorably oriented to interact with actin.
source: Assuming further that only those heads oriented towards one side, that is, one quarter, can interact with the actin filament, and that only one head of the head pair is favorably oriented to interact, we estimate the average number of interacting heads as 30 per myofilament.
evidence: Assumption used in model calculation

claim: Synthetic myofilaments fragment and compact membrane-bound actin while processively moving along actin filaments.
source: We show that synthetic myofilaments fragment and compact membrane-bound actin while processively moving along actin filaments.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from the abstract

claim: Tension builds up between the ends of myofilaments, resulting in compressive stress exerted to single actin filaments, causing their buckling and breakage.
source: We propose a mechanism by which tension builds up between the ends of myofilaments, resulting in compressive stress exerted to single actin filaments, causing their buckling and breakage.
evidence: Proposed mechanism from the abstract

claim: Modeling revealed that sufficient force (∼20 pN) can be generated by single myofilaments to buckle and break actin filaments.
source: Modeling of this mechanism revealed that sufficient force (∼20 pN) can be generated by single myofilaments to buckle and break actin filaments.
evidence: Modeling results from the abstract

claim: This mechanism of filament fragmentation and compaction may contribute to actin turnover and cortex reorganization during cytokinesis.
source: This mechanism of filament fragmentation and compaction may contribute to actin turnover and cortex reorganization during cytokinesis.
evidence: Proposed biological significance from the abstract
